1205.title: The Zahiris
1205.hook: the literalist school of Ibn Hazm, now small
1205.howItsDone: Zahiri jurists derive law only from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and sunnah, rejecting analogy (qiyas); the school is small today, but Ibn Hazm's books are still read by students of law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ibadis of Oman: a school with its own name, asking to be called by it.

A sign on a park gate says: no dogs. Someone walks in with a pet wolf. Is that allowed? One kind of reader reaches for the purpose behind the sign and says no, obviously. Another kind stops and asks: who decides what the sign meant beyond what it says? If the rule-maker wanted wolves kept out, couldn't the rule-maker have written it? That second reader isn't being silly. That reader is protecting the text from everyone's guesses. In Islamic law, that reader had a school, and its great voice lived in Muslim Spain. Today, the Zahiris.
screen: `NO DOGS. IN COMES A WOLF.` → `THE PURPOSE, OR THE WORDS?` → `A SCHOOL OF THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Zahir is Arabic for what's outward, what shows on the surface. The Zahiris are the people of the plain sense: the law is what the Qur'an and the sunnah actually say, read in their apparent meaning. Tradition names Dawud al-Zahiri of Baghdad as the founder. Next, the tool they put down. Other schools use qiyas, analogy: if wine is forbidden because it intoxicates, so is any drink that intoxicates. The Zahiris refused analogy as a source of law. Where the texts speak, follow them. Where they're silent, the matter is left open, and no jurist may close it with a guess. Then their great voice. Ibn Hazm of Cordoba wrote the method out at full length, in a book of law called al-Muhalla, arguing case by case. Tradition remembers him as sharp-tongued and fearless in debate, and he also wrote a book about love, The Ring of the Dove, full of lovers, glances and letters. Last, a test case. The Qur'an tells children, about aging parents, in Pickthall's words, "say not 'Fie' unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word." An analogist says: if even 'fie' is forbidden, striking a parent is forbidden all the more. A Zahiri agrees on the result, not the route. The same verses already command kindness, and other texts forbid harm. The plain sense is enough. The school is small today, but its question still sits in classrooms of fiqh: are you reading the text, or reading yourself into it?
screen: `ZAHIR: WHAT SHOWS ON THE SURFACE.` · `NO ANALOGY. SILENCE STAYS OPEN.` · `IBN HAZM OF CORDOBA.` · `NOT EVEN 'FIE.'`

segments.voice: Take one short message you got recently, a text, an email, a note on the fridge, and read it once exactly as written, nothing added. Then read it again with everything you know about the person who sent it, and notice the gap between the two readings, and how much of the second one you supplied yourself. If you pray, you can ask to read well.
The Zahiris. The school of the plain sense: the law is what the texts outwardly say, with no analogy to fill their silences. Today's word.
Your line: the plain sense. The words come first, and the guessing after. See you tomorrow.

1206.title: The Amman Message
1206.hook: in 2004 hundreds of scholars recognized the eight schools and forbade declaring their followers unbelievers
1206.howItsDone: The Amman Message and its three points recognize eight schools of law, the four Sunni schools with the Ja'fari, Zaydi, Ibadi and Zahiri, forbid declaring their followers unbelievers, and limit fatwas to those qualified in a school's method.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zahiris, the school of the plain sense. Your line: the plain sense.

One word can end a conversation for good. In Arabic it's takfir: declaring another Muslim an unbeliever. Said by the wrong person at the wrong time, it doesn't just insult. It can put a target on someone's back. Now, Amman, the capital of Jordan, and a different kind of sentence. Scholars from Sunni, Shia and Ibadi schools, people who disagree about hands in prayer, about the moon, about who should lead, put their names to a list of schools and said: these are all Muslims. Today, the Amman Message.
screen: `TAKFIR: CALLING A MUSLIM AN UNBELIEVER.` → `A ROOM IN AMMAN.` → `THESE ARE ALL MUSLIMS.`

segments.voice: In 2004, the Amman Message was issued in Jordan, under King Abdullah the Second, as a statement of what Islam is and is not. Then a question went to senior scholars of different schools, and their answers became three points. The first: the names. Whoever follows one of the four Sunni schools, Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i or Hanbali, or the Ja'fari, the Zaydi, the Ibadi or the Zahiri school, is a Muslim. That's eight, and the schools of these last few days are there by name. The second point is the word from the hook. It is not permitted, the Message says, to declare the followers of these schools unbelievers. Takfir is closed off between them. Hundreds of scholars endorsed those points, by the Message's own record. The third: who may speak. A fatwa, a formal legal opinion, belongs to people qualified in a school's method, and no one may issue one outside that method. It's a guard against anyone with a microphone deciding who's in and who's out. Under all three sits a verse the schools share, in Pickthall's words: "hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." The Message doesn't erase difference. The schools still pray with different hands and argue in their books. What it says is that the arguing happens inside one family. Eight schools, one ummah, one community of believers.
screen: `AMMAN, JORDAN: A MESSAGE.` · `EIGHT SCHOOLS, NAMED.` · `NO TAKFIR BETWEEN THEM.` · `ONLY THE QUALIFIED GIVE FATWAS.`

segments.voice: Say the eight names slowly, one per breath: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali, Ja'fari, Zaydi, Ibadi, Zahiri, and notice which ones you know a little now and which still feel like strangers. Then hold one person whose practice differs from yours, in any faith or none, with the thought: we disagree, and we're still neighbors. If you pray, you can pray for unity among those who pray.
The Amman Message. Issued in Jordan; scholars named eight schools of law, and forbade declaring their followers unbelievers. Today's word.
Your line: eight schools, one ummah. Next, how the schools actually differ, starting with the hands. That's today, done.

1207.title: Hands in prayer
1207.hook: folded on the chest, below the navel, or at the sides, depending on school
1207.howItsDone: In the standing of prayer, Hanafis hold the right hand over the left below the navel, Shafi'is below the chest, Hanbalis below the navel or as their school allows; Malikis following Malik's reported view, and Ja'fari, Zaydi and Ibadi Muslims, pray with their arms at their sides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Amman Message: eight schools named, and no takfir between them. Your line: eight schools, one ummah.

Stand at the back of a big mosque during prayer and watch the hands. One man has his right hand over his left, low, just under the navel. The man beside him holds his higher, near the chest. Two places down, someone's arms hang straight at his sides. Nobody turns to correct anybody. They bow together, go down together, rise together. Same prayer, same imam, three different pairs of hands. Each of them learned it from somewhere. Today, why.
screen: `WATCH THE HANDS.` → `LOW, HIGH, AT THE SIDES.` → `NOBODY CORRECTS ANYBODY.`

segments.voice: Start with a report the schools share. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahl ibn Sa'd says people were told to place the right hand on the left forearm in prayer. Holding, called qabd, has a text behind it. But the text leaves a question: where? It says right over left. It doesn't say how high. So the schools weighed other reports, and different answers came out. Hanafi scholars teach men to hold the hands below the navel. Shafi'i scholars place them below the chest and above the navel. In the Hanbali school, below the navel is a well-known view, with room for other places. And some readers point to reports placing the hands on the chest itself. Then the arms at the sides, called sadl, letting the hands hang. In the Maliki school, a report from Imam Malik is read as disliking holding in the obligatory prayers, and in Maliki mosques you may see arms down. The Ja'fari school teaches the arms at the sides, hands resting on the thighs, and so do the Zaydis and the Ibadis. Each of these is a reading of reports from the same Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, passed down by different teachers. In the same row, the man with low hands and the man with hanging arms are each praying as their own school teaches. A stranger's hands aren't a mistake. They're a map of who taught him.
screen: `SAHL: RIGHT HAND OVER LEFT.` · `THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY HOW HIGH.` · `SADL: THE ARMS AT THE SIDES.` · `HANDS ARE A MAP OF TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: If you pray, stand for a moment, place your hands where you learned to, and ask who taught you: a parent, an imam, a video, a friend. If you don't, let your hands rest wherever they fall, feel their weight, and think of someone who taught you to do something with them, tie a knot, hold a pen, knead dough. Stay with that person for a few breaths.
Hands in prayer. Held below the navel, below the chest, on the chest, or at the sides, depending on school; each passed down by a teacher. Today's word.
Your line: different hands. One row, many teachers. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1208.title: Saying amin
1208.hook: aloud or silently after the Fatiha, by school
1208.howItsDone: After the Fatiha, Shafi'i and Hanbali congregations say amin aloud in the loud prayers; Hanafis and Malikis say it quietly; in the Ja'fari school it is not said in the prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hands in prayer: low, high, or at the sides, each from a teacher. Your line: different hands.

The imam reaches the end of the Fatiha in a loud prayer. The last line rings out, and in some mosques the whole hall answers with one long word, rolling from the front rows to the back like a wave hitting a wall: aameen. Visitors sometimes jump. In another mosque, same line, same voice, and then nothing you can hear. Lips move, maybe. The hall is silent. Today, one word, and the ways it is said, or not said.
screen: `THE FATIHA ENDS.` → `A WAVE OF SOUND: AAMEEN.` → `ANOTHER HALL: SILENCE.`

segments.voice: The Fatiha closes, in Pickthall's words, "Not the (path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray." Right after that line comes amin, a short request that Allah answer what was just asked. It isn't a verse of the Qur'an; it's the response to one. Why it matters: in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that when the imam says amin, the people should say it too, because whoever's amin falls together with the amin of the angels has past sins forgiven. A small word, with a large promise around it. Then the question the report doesn't settle: how loud? Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars teach that in the loud prayers, the imam and those behind him say it aloud. That's the wave. They point to reports of the Prophet raising his voice with it. Hanafi scholars teach saying it quietly, as a supplication, and supplication, they say, is best kept low. Maliki teaching also keeps it quiet, with its own discussion of whether the imam says it in the loud prayers. Last, the Ja'fari school. Its jurists hold that amin is not part of the prayer, so it isn't said there at all; Shia worshippers pass straight from the Fatiha to the next surah. So one hall answers with a wave, another under the breath, and a third moves straight on.
screen: `AMIN: ANSWER WHAT WAS ASKED.` · `WITH THE AMIN OF THE ANGELS.` · `ALOUD, OR UNDER THE BREATH?` · `THE JA'FARI SCHOOL: NOT SAID.`

segments.voice: Sit quietly and think of one thing you hope for today, something small and real, and hold it. Notice the difference between saying a hope out loud and keeping it under your breath. If you pray, you can say amin in the way your school teaches.
Saying amin. The response after the Fatiha: aloud in loud prayers for Shafi'is and Hanbalis, quietly for Hanafis and Malikis, not said in the Ja'fari school. Today's word.
Your line: aloud or silent. The same word can be a wave or a whisper. Until tomorrow.

1209.title: Touching and wudu
1209.hook: schools differ on whether touching certain things breaks wudu
1209.howItsDone: Each school teaches its own list of what breaks wudu: in the Shafi'i school skin contact with an unrelated adult of the opposite sex does, in the Maliki and Hanbali schools only touch with desire, and in the Hanafi and Ja'fari schools touch alone does not.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saying amin: aloud, quietly, or not at all. Your line: aloud or silent.

A couple heads out the door for the evening prayer. Both have just made wudu, the washing before prayer: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, feet. At the door, one reaches for the other's hand. Then a pause. Does that touch mean washing again before praying? Ask a Shafi'i teacher, a Hanafi teacher and a Maliki teacher, and you may get three different answers, each with a verse and a report behind it. It sounds like the smallest question in the world. It's a doorway into how the schools read one word.
screen: `FRESH WUDU, OUT THE DOOR.` → `ONE HAND REACHES FOR ANOTHER.` → `WASH AGAIN, OR NOT?`

segments.voice: In surah five, the Qur'an lists the things after which a believer who can't find water should use clean earth instead, and one of them is a phrase built on the verb lamasa: when you have touched women. What does touched mean? A report from Ibn Abbas takes it as a polite way of naming intercourse, the way English says two people slept together. Others among the Companions, tradition says, took it as touch by hand. Hanafi scholars follow the first reading: a touch of the hand doesn't break wudu. They also point to Aisha's report in Sahih al-Bukhari: she lay in front of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ while he prayed at night, and when he went down to prostrate, he touched her feet so she would draw them in, and he kept praying. Shafi'i scholars take touched as touch: skin on skin with an unrelated adult of the opposite sex breaks wudu, desire or not. Maliki and Hanbali scholars stand between: the touch breaks wudu when it comes with desire. Ja'fari jurists hold that touching doesn't break it at all. Last, a second case, with two reports side by side. Busra bint Safwan reports that whoever touches his private part should make wudu. Talq ibn Ali reports the Prophet asking, isn't it just a part of you? Shafi'is and Hanbalis lean on Busra; Hanafis on Talq. The details differ. The washing stays.
screen: `ONE VERB: LAMASA, TO TOUCH.` · `A POLITE WORD, OR A HAND?` · `SHAFI'I, MALIKI, HANBALI, JA'FARI.` · `BUSRA AND TALQ, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: If you follow a school, ask yourself honestly whether you know what it teaches about touch and wudu. If you don't, recall one small rule you grew up with, shoes off at the door, no hat at the table, the first bite for the eldest, and ask whether you know the reason behind it. Hold the rule and its reason for a few breaths, without judging either.
Touching and wudu. Whether a touch breaks the washing before prayer: by one reading, it doesn't; by another, skin on skin does; by another, only with desire. Today's word.

1210.title: The moon
1210.hook: some sight the moon locally, some follow another country, some use calculation
1210.howItsDone: Mosques and councils start the Islamic months, including Ramadan and the Eids, by one of several methods: a local sighting of the crescent, following another country's announced sighting, or astronomical calculation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, touching and wudu: one verb, read more than one way. Your line: details differ.

Eid morning, and the group chat is arguing. One cousin is already in new clothes, posting photos from the mosque. Another is still fasting, because her mosque says the month has one more day. A third says his community decided weeks ago, by the numbers. Same city, same family, same Ramadan, and two different Eids. It all comes from one question about a crescent, answered more than one way. Today, the moon.
screen: `EID MORNING, THE CHAT IS ARGUING.` → `ONE COUSIN FEASTS, ONE FASTS.` → `ONE QUESTION, SEVERAL ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The Islamic months follow the moon, and the Qur'an says of the new moons, in Pickthall's words, "They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage." A month begins with the thin crescent, the hilal, just after sunset. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says: fast when you see it, and stop fasting when you see it, and if it's hidden from you, complete the month as thirty days. Seeing is at the heart of it. So, the first question: whose seeing? In Sahih Muslim, Kurayb travels from Syria to Medina. In Syria, he says, people saw the new moon on Friday night and began fasting. Ibn Abbas, in Medina, answers that they saw it on Saturday night and will keep counting by their own sighting. This is how we were told, he says. Some scholars read that as each region sighting its own moon. Others say one sighting anywhere binds everyone who hears of it, so some communities follow another country's announcement. The second question: what counts as seeing? Some jurists say an eye on the horizon, nothing else. Others answer that astronomers can now say ahead of time when the crescent will be born and when it can be seen, and that a reliable calculation can stand in for the eye, or at least rule out a mistaken sighting. Some councils announce the dates far in advance. So the family chat is arguing over three readings of one sentence about a crescent.

1211.title: Witr in many ways
1211.hook: one, three, or more units, prayed in different ways
1211.howItsDone: Witr is prayed after the night prayer and before dawn: Hanafis as three joined units with qunut, treating it as wajib; Shafi'is and Hanbalis as one or more odd units, often two and then one; Malikis as one unit after a pair; Ja'fari Shia as a single unit with qunut closing the night prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the moon: one crescent, counted more than one way. Your line: which moon?

It's late. The house is dark except for one lamp. Someone who has already prayed the night prayer stands up once more before bed, for one last short prayer. In one home it's three units, with a quiet supplication tucked inside the third. In another it's a single unit, standing alone. In a third, two units, a pause and a greeting of peace, and then one more. All three would tell you the same thing: they're closing the night with an odd number. Today, witr, the odd prayer, and the many ways to pray it.
screen: `ONE LAMP, ONE LAST PRAYER.` → `THREE, OR ONE, OR TWO THEN ONE.` → `ALWAYS AN ODD NUMBER.`

segments.voice: Witr means odd, the opposite of even. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that Allah is witr, one, and loves what is odd. The prayer carries the same word. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Umar reports the Prophet's answer: the night prayer is prayed two units by two, and when someone fears the dawn is near, they pray one unit to make the whole odd. And in Sunan Abi Dawud, a report gives the choice outright: whoever wishes may pray witr with five, or with three, or with one. The odd number is fixed. The shape is open. Then the schools. Hanafi scholars teach that witr is wajib, a duty just below the obligatory prayers, prayed as three units joined with one closing greeting, and a supplication, the qunut, before bowing in the third. Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars count it as a strongly encouraged sunna; its smallest form is a single unit, and three may be prayed as two, a greeting, then one. Maliki teaching has a single unit of witr, following a pair of units prayed first. In the Ja'fari school, witr is a single unit that closes the night prayer, with a qunut of its own. Each of these is odd, and each closes the night. The people in those three homes stand at different angles to the same instruction, and each can show you the report they're standing on.
screen: `WITR: ODD, NOT EVEN.` · `TWO BY TWO, THEN ONE.` · `FIVE, THREE, OR ONE.` · `EACH SCHOOL'S SHAPE.`
